docs.title: Lab infrastructure
docs.text:
How the Societal Analytics Lab (VU Amsterdam) hosts its tools: the login service, the lab's own research software (AmCAT, AnnoTinder), and tools for lab members, such as transcription. This describes what we do, not how to do it in general: we assume you know your way around a Linux server.

Page What Our servers Which servers we have, and what runs where Setting up a server Admin accounts, firewall, Docker, /opt, backups: the same on every server Docker Compose The settings every app uses, and the pitfalls Apps Each app: what it is, and the commands to run it FAQ Why we do it this way

docs.title: In short
docs.text:
• Every app runs with Docker Compose, in its own folder /opt/<app>, with everything needed to restore it in that folder.
  • Only HTTPS is public. Each server has one reverse proxy (Caddy) in front of its apps; apps only listen on the server itself.
  • One login service, Keycloak at auth.societal-analytics.nl, for everything that needs a login. Apps without a login of their own sit behind the lab portal.
  • Backups: every server backs up /opt every night, encrypted, with the database dumps the apps make themselves, and copies that off-site. VU IT's server backups are the last resort.
  • Everything we make is open source, our deployments included: github.com/vu-societal-analytics. The exception is our Keycloak configuration, the most sensitive part: its repository is private.

docs.text:
Browser session authentication is managed by an OIDC provider capable of handling enterprise and institutional security requirements. The OIDC provider only does authentication: letting users securely prove to AmCAT that they own an email address.

For University hosted AmCAT servers we recommend the institution's own identity provider. See the Authentication standard for the requirements, and Authentication provider for teams that host AmCAT themselves.

docs.title: Infrastructure Details
docs.text:
• Proxy: Caddy serving on Port 443.
  • Frontend: Vite-built React SPA served at /.
  • Backend API: FastAPI server mounted at /api.
  • OIDC flow: Initiated and callback on Backend; tokens set as signed, http-only session cookie
  • Data Storage (ES): ElasticSearch, used for both metadata and primary textual data storage.
  • Object Storage (S3): S3-compatible storage for large files.
  • Deployment Note: FastAPI, ElasticSearch, and S3 are decoupled and may reside on different physical or virtual servers.

docs.title: Keycloak
docs.text:
The login service, at auth.societal-analytics.nl: Keycloak with PostgreSQL, its own Caddy, and an email relay. Repository: deploy-keycloak, which is private: it holds the login flows and settings of every realm, the most sensitive part of our setup. The server reads it with a read-only deploy key, and builds its two images itself (Keycloak prepared for a quick start, and Caddy with a rate limit module):

# after adding the server's deploy key to the repository (INSTALL.md, "Files and settings")
sudo -u keycloak git clone ssh://git@ssh.github.com:443/vu-societal-analytics/deploy-keycloak.git /opt/keycloak && cd /opt/keycloak
sudo -u keycloak cp .env.example .env && sudo -u keycloak chmod 600 .env      # then fill it in
sudo docker compose up -d --build

Everything else (the admin hostname and its IP restriction, the realms, upgrades, recovery) is in the repository's INSTALL.md. The Keycloak folder is owned by its own system account keycloak, not by sal.

docs.title: Lab portal
docs.text:
The start page of the lab server, at lab.societal-analytics.nl, and the server's reverse proxy: Caddy, plus a small app that signs people in with Keycloak, handles lab membership (requests, invitations, approval by lab admins), and adds that login to the lab apps that have none. Which apps it serves, and who may use them, is set in config/services.yml; the lab admins in config/admins.yml. Repository: deploy-lab-portal (compose.yml).

mkdir -p config caddy && V=v0.1.0 && R=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vu-societal-analytics/deploy-lab-portal/$V
curl -fsSLO $R/compose.yml
curl -fsSL -o .env $R/.env.example && chmod 600 .env                 # then fill it in
curl -fsSL -o config/services.yml $R/config/services.example.yml
curl -fsSL -o config/admins.yml $R/config/admins.example.yml
mkdir -p data backups && sudo chown 1000:1000 data backups caddy
sudo docker compose pull && sudo docker compose up -d

The Keycloak client, the first admin, and adding an app: the README. An app behind the portal is one entry in config/services.yml, e.g.:

services:
  whisper:                       # https://whisper.lab.societal-analytics.nl
    name: Whisper
    description: Transcription of audio
    upstream: 127.0.0.1:9000     # the port the app publishes on 127.0.0.1
    access: members              # members, admins, or public (an app with its own login)
    mfa: required                # only with a second factor
    max_upload: 2.5GB
    timeout: 3000s
    # session_idle: 8h           # own session limits instead of 30m / 12h, e.g. for a notebook server

Backups are Elasticsearch's own snapshots, in ./backups. Once, after the first start, register that folder and schedule a daily snapshot, kept 7 days:

read -rsp 'Password of elastic: ' P && echo
es() { curl -s -u "elastic:$P" -H Content-Type:application/json "http://<internal address>:9200$1" "${@:2}"; echo; }
es /_snapshot/backups -X PUT -d '{"type":"fs","settings":{"location":"/backups"}}'
es /_slm/policy/daily -X PUT -d '{"schedule":"0 30 1 * * ?","name":"<daily-{now/d}>","repository":"backups","config":{"include_global_state":true},"retention":{"expire_after":"7d","min_count":1,"max_count":14}}'
es /_slm/policy/daily/_execute -X POST

Restoring an index, after deleting or closing it: es /_snapshot/backups/<snapshot>/_restore -X POST -d '{"indices":"<index>"}' (the snapshots: es /_cat/snapshots/backups).

docs.title: Authentication provider
docs.text:
Our software doesn't handle passwords or second factors itself: it delegates logins to an OIDC provider (see the Authentication standard). This page is for teams that host AmCAT or AnnoTinder themselves, and need to choose that provider.

What the lab uses: its own Keycloak, for the lab's own servers (Keycloak). It is not a service for other teams' servers, but its setup and realm files (deploy-keycloak) can serve as an example if you decide to run your own Keycloak.

What the provider must do (requirements): verify email addresses, support 2FA and signal it to the server, and support step-up (max_age and auth_time). Which provider fits depends on your institution and on the data on your server:

  1. Your institution's identity provider, or another provider that meets the requirements. Required for sensitive research data.
  2. For teaching and other servers without sensitive data: a provider that doesn't meet all requirements, with weaker security settings.

Your team is responsible for the personal data on your server, and needs its own privacy statement; the lab's privacy statement can serve as an example. Moving to another provider later is a migration.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
The safest choice is a provider that is managed by a security team and has a helpdesk for account recovery: for most universities, the institution's own identity provider. Talk to your IT department: they decide which providers may be used for research data, and may already have one available.

Provider 2FA signal (OIDC_MFA_CLAIM) Notes Your institution's identity provider Depends on the provider Recommended for research data. Ask your IT department. SURFconext (Dutch institutions) acr:<SURFsecureID LoA> 2FA via SURFsecureID, which institutions procure separately. Arranged by your institution. SURF SRAM (Dutch institutions) TODO: verify For research collaborations, including members from other institutions (eduGAIN) and guests (eduID). Every user logs in with 2FA. Microsoft Entra ID, Google Workspace amr:mfa Institutional accounts. Entra ID needs amr as an optional claim; Google only includes amr when the information is available, so test it. ZITADEL Cloud amr:mfa (verify) Free plan for small teams (100 daily active users), EU data region. You handle account recovery yourself. Use one instance per team. Self-hosted Keycloak amr:mfa Like the lab's own. Only as secure as its maintenance: someone has to keep it updated and handle account recovery.

Not suitable where 2FA is required: the Auth0 free plan (no step-up) and Google consumer accounts (@gmail.com, no institutional agreements, and amr is not always present). The 2FA signals were checked in November 2026 (details and sources); provider behaviour changes, so test the setup before going live. The full evaluation, including Authentik and Auth0: Provider comparison.

docs.title: Teaching and low-sensitivity servers
docs.text:
For a server without sensitive data, such as a course or a pilot, a provider that doesn't meet all requirements can be used, with one or both of the weaker security settings:

  • AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true when the provider has no 2FA, or can't signal it. Sensitive actions (API keys, changing roles) then only need a recent login. Everyone understands the limitation: whoever has a user's password can act as that user.
  • AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true only when the provider does verify email addresses but doesn't send email_verified. Never with a provider where users can choose an address without proving they own it: roles given to an email address could then be claimed by someone else.

Both settings show a permanent warning on the admin page. If the server later gets sensitive data, choose a provider that meets the requirements and migrate first.

docs.title: Checklist for your own provider
docs.text:
• The provider is approved by your institution for the data on your server.
  • The provider returns email_verified: true for your users.
  • 2FA is required (or can be requested) for your users, and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM matches the provider's signal. (Or, for a teaching server only: AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true.)
  • Step-up works: a sensitive action (e.g. creating an API key) more than AUTH_STEP_UP_IDLE after the login or the last sensitive action, or more than AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE after the login, asks for 2FA again.
  • It is clear who handles account recovery for your users (a helpdesk, or your own admin).
  • The server admin page shows no hardening warnings, or only the ones you chose deliberately.
  • If you are moving from another provider: follow the Migration guide.

docs.title: Migration guide: changing OIDC providers
docs.text: This guide is for teams that move their AmCAT or AnnoTinder server to a different OIDC provider, for instance from a hosted provider used for a pilot to their institution's provider. The person hosting the server is responsible for the migration.

docs.title: Why migration needs care
docs.text:
The OIDC provider is the source of truth for the identity of a user. Our software identifies users by the combination of iss (the provider) and sub (the user at that provider), not by email address (see IBAC). A new provider means a new iss and new sub values, so without a migration the server will not recognize existing users, and all their roles are lost.

There are two strategies:

Account linking JIT re-claiming How users keep their account They link their new login while still logged in with the old one They log in with the new provider and re-claim their account via their email address Relies on email No Yes Both providers needed Yes, during a transition period No Effort for users One extra login during the transition period None Best for Servers with important data, as long as the old provider is still available Servers without sensitive data, or when the old provider is no longer available

docs.title: Account linking
docs.text:
Account linking is the industry standard way to migrate. A user can have multiple login identities (see the identities table in IBAC), so a user can add their new login to their existing account. Because the user is authenticated at both providers when linking, email plays no role.

Steps

  1. Register your server at the new provider, and check it against the checklist.
  2. Move the current provider settings to the OIDC_PREVIOUS_* variables, set the new provider in the OIDC_* variables, and choose an end date in OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL (e.g. three months ahead). See Configuration.
  3. Users can now log in with either provider. Users who log in with the old provider are asked to link their new login: they sign in at the new provider, and the server adds the new identity to their account.
  4. Remind users before the end date. Server admins can see which users have not linked yet.
  5. After OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL, the old provider is no longer accepted. Remove the OIDC_PREVIOUS_* variables. Users who did not link can still re-claim their account (see below).

docs.title: JIT re-claiming
docs.text:
With JIT re-claiming, the server forgets the old identities, and users re-claim their account based on their verified email address, using the same JIT account claiming mechanism we use for invitations.

Steps

  1. Register your server at the new provider, and check it against the checklist.
  2. Set the new provider in the OIDC_* variables.
  3. TODO: admin command that removes all identities, turning existing users into shadow users that can be claimed by email.
  4. Users log in with the new provider. If their verified email address matches an existing user, they claim that account.

Risks

Re-claiming relies on email ownership. Someone who controls a user's email address at the new provider (for instance after an address was reassigned) can claim that user's account and roles. Our safeguards limit this: email verification is required (don't use JIT re-claiming with AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION), roles of dormant users are disabled, and unclaimed accounts expire after 3 months. But the risk is not eliminated, so prefer account linking for servers with important data.

For a server without sensitive data (e.g. a teaching server) this is usually acceptable. It is also the fallback for users who missed the account linking transition period.

docs.title: Authentication standard
docs.text:
How authentication works in all software developed by the Societal Analytics Lab (AmCAT, AnnoTinder): what the software does, and what it requires from the OIDC provider. It is written for developers of our software. Teams that host the software only need parts of it; these pages link to those:

  • Authentication provider: for teams that host our software.
  • Migration guide: moving to a different OIDC provider.
  • Decisions: why it is set up this way, and which alternatives we dropped.

docs.title: OpenID Connect (OIDC)
docs.text:
OIDC is an open standard for authentication that builds on top of the OAuth 2.0 protocol. It allows clients to verify the identity of users based on the authentication performed by an external identity provider (IdP). By using OIDC, our software does not handle user authentication directly, but delegates it to an external OIDC provider. This is an industry standard, because it outsources the hard part of authentication to a dedicated provider, which is often better equipped to handle it than the application itself.

Our software works with any OIDC provider that meets the provider requirements. The person hosting our software chooses the provider, and is responsible for making sure it is suitable. The safest choice is a provider that is managed by a security team and has a helpdesk for account recovery. Talk to your institution's IT support circle.

docs.title: Choosing an OIDC provider
docs.text:
The person hosting our software chooses the OIDC provider (see Authentication provider):

  • Your institution's identity provider (recommended, and the right choice for sensitive research data): managed by a security team, with a helpdesk for account recovery.
  • Another provider that meets the requirements, hosted (e.g. ZITADEL Cloud) or self-hosted (e.g. Keycloak). The lab runs its own Keycloak for its own servers; its documentation (Keycloak) can serve as an example.
  • For teaching and other servers without sensitive data: a provider that doesn't meet all requirements, with the weaker security settings turned on.

Names and email addresses of users (e.g. students) are personal data, so any server must be used according to your institution's rules. Moving to another provider is a migration. For development on a local machine there is a separate development mode.

docs.title: OIDC provider requirements
docs.text:
By default, the provider must meet all three requirements. The first two can be turned off, for teaching and other servers without sensitive data (see Weaker security).

Requirement What the provider must do Email verification Return "email_verified": true in the ID token. Our software uses email addresses to assign roles (see Authorization). 2FA with a usable signal Support 2FA, and signal in the ID token that it was used. Providers do this differently (amr containing mfa, or a specific acr value), so the claim is configured with OIDC_MFA_CLAIM. See Provider support for MFA signals. Step-up Honour the max_age parameter (re-authenticate if the last login is older than N seconds), and return auth_time in the ID token. This one can't be turned off.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Proposed names; to be aligned with the AmCAT and AnnoTinder code.

Variable Required Description OIDC_HOST yes Issuer URL of the trusted OIDC provider. OIDC_CLIENT_ID yes Client ID registered at the provider. OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET yes Client secret registered at the provider. OIDC_MFA_CLAIM no Which claim counts as 2FA: amr:mfa (default) or acr:<value>, e.g. acr:http://test.surfconext.nl/assurance/loa2 for SURFconext. AUTH_SESSION_IDLE, AUTH_SESSION_MAX no The application's own session: seconds without activity, and seconds in total, before the user signs in again (see Sessions and signing out). Default: 1800 and 86400 (30 minutes, 24 hours). AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE, AUTH_STEP_UP_IDLE no Sensitive actions: the maximum age in seconds of the last 2FA login, and the seconds since that login or the last sensitive action (see Two-factor authentication). Default: 3600 and 900 (1 hour, 15 minutes). OIDC_PREVIOUS_HOST, OIDC_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_ID, OIDC_PREVIOUS_CLIENT_SECRET, OIDC_PREVIOUS_MFA_CLAIM no The previous OIDC provider, only during a migration. OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL no Date after which the previous provider is no longer accepted. AUTH_DEV_MODE no Enables development mode. Refused unless the server only listens on localhost. AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA no true turns off the 2FA requirement (see Weaker security). AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION no true turns off the email verification requirement (see Weaker security).

docs.title: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
docs.text:
For sensitive actions (e.g. creating API keys, changing roles) our servers require a recent 2FA login (step-up authentication), in a window like GitHub's "sudo mode": the login is at most AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE old (1 hour), and at most AUTH_STEP_UP_IDLE (15 minutes) has passed since that login or the last sensitive action. Each sensitive action renews that 15 minutes, so a batch of admin work needs one login, not one per change. (OWASP's verification standard requires a recent login or re-authentication before sensitive actions, without prescribing a window; 15 minutes is OWASP's idle timeout for high-value applications, at the strict end.)

  1. The server checks OIDC_MFA_CLAIM and auth_time in the ID token of the session's login, and when the last sensitive action was.
  2. If the claim is missing or the window has passed, the server sends the user to the OIDC provider for a new login, with max_age=0 and prompt=login (Keycloak skips max_age=0 when the last login was within the same second; prompt=login always asks).
  3. The server checks the new ID token itself, because providers do not always enforce what was requested.

With AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA, steps 1 to 3 only check auth_time: sensitive actions still need a recent login, but not a second factor.

Account recovery (e.g. a lost phone) is the responsibility of the OIDC provider.

docs.title: Weaker security: teaching and low-sensitivity servers
docs.text:
Two requirements can be turned off, each with its own setting. Both are deliberately named INSECURE: they make the server less secure, and must never be used for servers with sensitive research data. In .env:

# Weaker security: only for teaching and other servers without sensitive data.
# See https://vu-societal-analytics.github.io/societal-analytics-lab-infra/auth/#weaker-security-teaching-and-low-sensitivity-servers
AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true
AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true

AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA=true

  • Sensitive actions (e.g. creating API keys, changing roles) no longer require a second factor, but still require a recent login (step-up with max_age and auth_time).
  • The server still records whether a login used 2FA (has_mfa, with OIDC_MFA_CLAIM), so admins can see who uses it anyway.
  • Risk: anyone who gets hold of a user's password, or their email (to reset it), can perform that user's sensitive actions.

AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION=true

  • Users can log in when the provider doesn't confirm their email address (email_verified is false or missing). The server records what the provider sent (email_verified in the user table).
  • Roles given to an email address (invitations, see JIT account claiming) can still be claimed by a user whose address is not verified. That is the risk: on a provider where people can choose their own address, someone could claim the roles meant for someone else. Only use this setting with a provider that does verify addresses but doesn't send the claim (e.g. some institutional providers).
  • Roles based on the email domain, or on having a verified address (ABAC, require_email), still only apply to users with email_verified = true.

Both settings:

  • The server logs a warning at every start.
  • The admin page permanently shows them as hardening warnings.
  • Turning a setting off again restores the requirement: users who don't meet it can no longer log in (email) or perform sensitive actions (2FA).

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Our software also supports direct API access via API keys. These are application-managed tokens that are decoupled from the OIDC provider.

  • API keys can only be created and changed by the main web client, in a session that passed step-up authentication.
  • API keys always have a limited scope.

docs.title: Server hardening warnings
docs.text:
The web client shows server admins a list of warnings for things that make the server less secure:

Warning Meaning 2FA not required AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA is set: sensitive actions don't need a second factor. Not for sensitive data (see Weaker security). Email verification not required AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION is set. Not for sensitive data. Roles for unverified email addresses Users with roles whose provider did not confirm their email address (email_verified = false). Check that these are the right people. No 2FA signal Recent logins did not contain the configured OIDC_MFA_CLAIM, so sensitive actions are blocked. Check the provider's 2FA settings and OIDC_MFA_CLAIM. (Not shown with AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA.) Migration not finished OIDC_PREVIOUS_HOST is still configured after OIDC_PREVIOUS_UNTIL.

docs.title: Development mode
docs.text:
AUTH_DEV_MODE lets developers run our software on their own machine without an OIDC provider, logged in as a local admin. The server refuses to start in development mode unless it only listens on localhost. Development mode is never used for servers that other people use.

An app may let you choose the test user in development mode (for instance with a sign-in form where you type any email address, with or without a second factor), so you can try how it behaves for different users.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
All software developed by the Societal Analytics Lab follows these rules, to ensure consistency and security across our software stack.

Rule Details Same origin The server and web client are always hosted on the same domain. Server-side OIDC flow The server initiates and completes the OIDC flow with the trusted provider (OIDC_HOST), and sets a signed, http-only session cookie. Scopes The server requests the scopes openid email, nothing more. It uses sub, email, email_verified, the 2FA signal and auth_time, and no name, so users aren't asked to share more than needed. One session per application When AmCAT and AnnoTinder are hosted together, each application has its own session. They can share one OIDC client (the same client ID and client secret), so that users consent once per host (see One client per host). The second login completes without user interaction, while the user is still signed in at the provider. Own session, sign-out The application's session is independent of the provider's session: 30 minutes idle, 24 hours at most, configurable. Signing out ends it and the provider's session (see Sessions and signing out). Authorization on the server The server decides what users may do, not the OIDC provider (see Authorization). API keys for other clients Other clients (e.g. R or Python) can only access the backend via API keys. Email verification The server checks the email_verified claim, unless AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION is set (see Weaker security). 2FA and step-up The server checks OIDC_MFA_CLAIM and auth_time for sensitive actions, and performs step-up authentication if needed (see Two-factor authentication). AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_2FA drops the OIDC_MFA_CLAIM check, not the step-up.

docs.title: Sessions and signing out
docs.text:
There are three kinds of session, and keeping them apart is what makes signing in and out behave as users expect:

  1. The provider's session (in Keycloak: the user session): the browser's login at the provider. While it lasts, every application of the realm can sign the user in without a password. That is useful for single sign-on (from AmCAT to AnnoTinder in one click), and a risk on a shared computer: someone who signed in to one application and only closed it leaves a login behind for all of them. So our provider keeps it short: 10 minutes without activity, at most 30 minutes.
  2. The provider's client sessions: one per application, inside the provider's session. Ordinary refresh tokens belong to them, so they stop working when the provider's session ends, including when the user signs out in any application.
  3. The application's own session: its session cookie.

The rule: an application's session must not depend on the provider's session. Otherwise one application's sign-out, or a short provider session, would end every application's session in the middle of someone's work. So an application either:

  • keeps its own session after the login (our software: the server uses OIDC once to sign the user in, and needs no refresh token), or
  • requests offline_access: a refresh token that is independent of the provider's session (it survives a sign-out elsewhere). Tools that keep users signed in with refresh tokens (e.g. oauth2-proxy, by adding offline_access to its scopes) do it this way. In our Keycloak, a client gets it only when it asks, with the session limits of its client settings.

How long a session lasts: an idle timeout and an absolute timeout (OWASP, Session Management), within the limits of NIST SP 800-63B-4 for logins with a second factor (at most 1 hour of inactivity, at most 24 hours in total):

Level Without activity In total Settings The session 30 minutes 24 hours AUTH_SESSION_IDLE, AUTH_SESSION_MAX Sensitive actions (within the session) 15 minutes since the 2FA login or the last sensitive action 1 hour since the 2FA login AUTH_STEP_UP_IDLE, AUTH_STEP_UP_MAX_AGE

An application whose use requires more may set more, and documents why: e.g. a notebook server that computes for hours while the user does nothing.

Continuing a task without a session: an application may let one specific task continue without a login session, when the login was only needed to start it: e.g. continuing a coding job in AnnoTinder on the device where it was opened. That permission must be limited to that one task (and preferably that device), and grant nothing else. There is no general "remember me": that is what the short sessions are for.

Signing out in an application:

  1. ends the application's own session;
  2. sends the browser to the provider's end-session endpoint, with the ID token of the login (id_token_hint, so the server keeps the ID token with the session) and a post_logout_redirect_uri. This ends the provider's session, so the next visit to any application asks for the password again.

Other applications are not affected by a sign-out: their own sessions continue. Applications don't depend on each other's sign-out, and OIDC's back-channel logout (the provider telling every application to end its session) is not used: it would make them dependent again.

Locking someone out (e.g. a compromised account): block them in the applications themselves (e.g. remove their role), and disable them at the provider, so they can't sign in again anywhere. Revoking their offline sessions at the provider ends the sessions of tools that use offline_access.

The lab portal does all of this, and is a short example to follow.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: Authorization is based on roles. A role can be given to a specific user (IBAC), to users with a certain attribute (ABAC), or both.

docs.title: Role table
docs.text: Column Description role What role a user has (e.g. READ, WRITE, ADMIN). context The context in which the role applies (e.g. project, server). user_id If not null, the role is linked to a specific user (see IBAC). email_domain If not null, the user's verified email (email_verified = true) must have this domain (see ABAC). Can be combined with user_id to require both. require_email If user_id and email_domain are null: whether any user gets the role (false), or only users with a verified email address (true). granted_at When the role was granted (created, updated, or restored).

docs.title: Identity Based Access Control (IBAC)
docs.text:
IBAC is the primary mode of authorization: roles are given to registered users.

The identity is iss + sub, not the email address. An email address is not a unique identifier, because it can change over time: users can change email addresses, and old email addresses can be reassigned. We do use the email address as a human readable way to assign roles (e.g. giving a colleague access to a project in AmCAT). This is safe, because the role is not assigned to the email address itself, but to the user (iss + sub) that currently owns it. Changing email addresses is the responsibility of the OIDC provider: when the email for an identity has changed, the server updates the user table.

Any user that signs in is registered, optionally with a form that collects additional information. We use this for security logs and rate limiting, which is legitimate under GDPR. Email addresses add some accountability, especially when roles require an email domain.

User table

Column Description id Unique user ID. email Email address of the user, from the most recent login. email_verified Whether the provider confirmed the email address at the most recent login: true only if it sent email_verified: true, otherwise false. NULL for shadow users. Without AUTH_INSECURE_DISABLE_EMAIL_VERIFICATION, only users with true can log in. has_mfa Whether the most recent login contained the 2FA signal (OIDC_MFA_CLAIM). Shown on the admin page, without a warning: 2FA is only needed for sensitive actions. registered_at When the user first signed in. NULL for shadow users until the account is claimed (see JIT account claiming). last_login_at When the user last signed in. reactivated_at First login after 1 year of inactivity. ... Optional user details (e.g. added on registration).

Identities table

Column Description user_id The user this identity belongs to. iss Issuer of the OIDC provider. sub Unique subject identifier at the OIDC provider. linked_at When the identity was linked to the user. last_login_at When the user last signed in with this identity.

Normally a user has one identity. A user can have more than one during a migration to a new OIDC provider.

docs.title: JIT account claiming
docs.text: Just-In-Time (JIT) account claiming lets us give roles to an email address that is not yet registered. The role is given to a new shadow user, which only has an id and email (registered_at is NULL, and there is no identity yet). The current owner of the email address is invited to claim the account and role. This can be an actual invitation, or just happen automatically when they first sign in. Claiming adds an identity and sets registered_at.

docs.title: Safeguards against email reassignment
docs.text:
Two safeguards prevent giving a role to a previous or future owner of an email address. A role is not given to a user if one of these conditions is true:

Dormant users. A role is disabled when:

role.granted_at < user.reactivated_at AND NOT user.has_mfa
  • Why: without 2FA, the OIDC provider only verifies current ownership of the email address. So after a year of inactivity, roles granted before reactivation are disabled. With 2FA required this should be rare, but it remains a safeguard for accounts claimed via email and providers that report 2FA inconsistently.
  • Restore: per role (e.g. an AmCAT project ADMIN refreshes granted_at), or by a server admin.

Expired invitations. A role is not given when:

user.registered_at > role.granted_at + INTERVAL '3 months'
  • Why: a role given to an unregistered email address must be claimed within 3 months, so that a future owner of the address can't claim it. Roles granted after registration are not affected, because then granted_at is later than registered_at.
  • Unclaimed invitations: a shadow user that is still unclaimed (registered_at IS NULL) has an expired invitation when now() > role.granted_at + INTERVAL '3 months'.
  • Restore: remove the invitation, or restore it by updating granted_at.

docs.title: Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC)
docs.text:
ABAC is the secondary mode of authorization: roles are given based on user attributes from OIDC claims. We currently only use the email domain, because this keeps the role of the OIDC provider restricted to authentication and email verification. In the future we could include other attributes (e.g. eduPerson claims from institutional providers).

IBAC and ABAC serve different purposes:

IBAC ABAC Based on Identities, tied to specific users Attributes, properties of users that can change Use Users keep their roles when they change email addresses. Important for long-term projects where researchers change institutions. Give and take away access based on a user's current situation, such as their affiliation with an institution.

Email domains are useful for:

  • Convenience: give access to anyone with an institutional email address, instead of giving everyone individual access. This should have limited privileges (never ADMIN).
  • Security: restrict access to a trusted institution. Combined with IBAC, access is restricted to a trusted person who also has a verified email address at that institution.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text: Every app runs from one compose.yml in /opt/<app>. The goal: if an app is compromised, it can't reach the server or the other apps, and everything needed to restore it is in its folder.

docs.title: The settings
docs.text:
An example with everything an app may need: the app, its database, a daily dump of that database, and (for a server with only this app) its own Caddy. Everything is in this one file, so a server needs nothing else besides .env.

name: example

x-logging: &logging              # logs rotate, so they can't fill the disk
  driver: json-file
  options: { max-size: 10m, max-file: "3" }

services:
  app:
    image: ghcr.io/example/app:1.2.3   # a fixed version, never "latest"
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *logging
    env_file: .env                     # settings and secrets (chmod 600)
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"          # only for the reverse proxy on this server
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/data               # files that must be kept: backed up
    networks: [default, db]
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }
    # Isolation: no root, no extra privileges, no writes outside its volumes
    user: "1000:1000"
    read_only: true
    tmpfs: [/tmp]
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    mem_limit: 1g

  db:
    image: postgres:18.7-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *logging
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: app
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD:?set POSTGRES_PASSWORD in .env}
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/postgresql    # a named volume: not in our backups (the dumps are)
    networks: [db]                     # only the app and the backup reach it; no internet
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U app"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 10

  db-backup:
    # A dump at the start and every day at 02:00 (UTC) into ./backups, kept 7 days
    image: postgres:18.7-alpine        # the same version as the database
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *logging
    entrypoint: ["/bin/sh", "/db-backup.sh"]
    configs:
      - source: db-backup
        target: /db-backup.sh
    environment:
      PGHOST: db
      PGUSER: app
      PGPASSWORD: ${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}
      PGDATABASE: app
      BACKUP_TIME: "02:00"
      KEEP_DAYS: 7
    volumes:
      - ./backups:/backups
    networks: [db]
    depends_on:
      db: { condition: service_healthy }

  caddy:
    # Only with COMPOSE_PROFILES=caddy in .env: HTTPS for a server with no other reverse proxy
    image: caddy:2.11.9-alpine
    profiles: [caddy]
    restart: unless-stopped
    logging: *logging
    network_mode: host                 # the one exception: see Pitfalls
    configs:
      - source: caddyfile
        target: /etc/caddy/Caddyfile
    volumes:
      - caddy-data:/data               # certificates: keep them (Let's Encrypt has rate limits)

volumes:
  db-data:
  caddy-data:

networks:
  db:
    internal: true

configs:
  caddyfile:
    content: |
      ${PUBLIC_HOST:?set PUBLIC_HOST in .env} {
        reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080
      }
  db-backup:
    # $$ is a literal $ (Compose fills in ${...} from .env)
    content: |
      set -eu
      umask 077
      time="$${BACKUP_TIME:-02:00}"; keep="$${KEEP_DAYS:-7}"
      hours="$${time%%:*}"; minutes="$${time##*:}"
      at=$$(( $${hours#0} * 3600 + $${minutes#0} * 60 ))   # "08" would be read as octal
      dump() {
        file="/backups/$$PGDATABASE-$$(date -u +%Y%m%d).dump"
        if pg_dump --format=custom $${DUMP_OPTIONS:-} > "$$file.partial"; then
            mv "$$file.partial" "$$file"; echo "$$(date -u -Iseconds) dump written: $$file"
        else
            rm -f "$$file.partial"; echo "$$(date -u -Iseconds) ERROR: pg_dump failed" >&2
        fi
        find /backups -name "$$PGDATABASE-*.dump" -type f -mtime +"$$((keep - 1))" -delete
      }
      until pg_isready -q; do sleep 5; done
      dump
      while true; do
        now=$$(date -u +%s); next=$$(( now - now % 86400 + at ))
        [ "$$next" -gt "$$now" ] || next=$$(( next + 86400 ))
        sleep $$(( next - now )); dump
      done

In short:

Setting Why A fixed image version Upgrades happen when we choose, after reading the release notes Ports only on 127.0.0.1 Only the reverse proxy on this server reaches the app (Pitfalls) An internal network for the database The database can't be reached by other containers, and can't reach the internet user, read_only, cap_drop, no-new-privileges A compromised app can't gain rights or change its own files. Use them where the image allows it: official database images need their default capabilities to start mem_limit, log rotation One app can't take the server's memory or disk ./data for files to keep, ./backups for dumps, named volumes for the rest Our backup of /opt contains exactly what's needed to restore the app (Setting up a server) configs: with content: Small config files live in the compose file itself: one file to download and to read

docs.title: A database with daily dumps
docs.text: A running database's own files can't be backed up reliably, so the database stays in a named volume, and the db-backup service above dumps it every day into ./backups. The server's nightly backup fails (and so emails us) when a backups/ folder has no dump from the last 26 hours.

docs.title: Restoring a database dump
docs.text:
From the app's folder; this replaces the database with the dump:

sudo docker compose stop app db-backup
sudo docker compose exec -T db dropdb -U app app
sudo docker compose exec -T db createdb -U app app
sudo cat backups/<dump> | sudo docker compose exec -T db pg_restore -U app -d app --no-owner
sudo docker compose up -d

An older dump: restore it from the nightly backup first (deploy-backup). Test a restore once when setting up an app.

Data that may only be kept for a limited time

E.g. uploaded audio and transcripts. Put it in a named volume (so it isn't in our backups), and delete it with a cleanup service in the same compose file, or with the app's own retention setting if it has one:

services:
  cleanup:
    # Every hour, delete uploads not changed for 30 days
    image: busybox:1.37
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: >
      sh -c 'while true; do
               find /uploads -type f -mtime +30 -delete;
               find /uploads -mindepth 1 -type d -empty -delete;
               sleep 3600;
             done'
    volumes:
      - uploads:/uploads

Only for a folder with nothing else in it (no settings, no database). Test it first with -mmin +10.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Published ports bypass the firewall. Docker forwards traffic to containers around the server's own firewall rules, so "8080:8080" is open to the whole internet, whatever the firewall says. Always "127.0.0.1:8080:8080", or no port at all for containers that only talk to each other. Check after every change; nothing should show 0.0.0.0: or [::]: except the reverse proxy's 80 and 443:

    sudo docker ps --format '{{.Names}}\t{{.Ports}}'

  • network_mode: host puts a container on the server's own network: it reaches everything on 127.0.0.1, including the other apps. Never for apps. The one exception is the reverse proxy, which reaches all apps anyway (Caddy in an app's compose file, and the lab portal's Caddy).

  • The docker group is root access: anyone who can run Docker can mount the whole disk into a container. Use sudo, and don't add anyone (or sal) to the group.
  • Missing folders for bind mounts (./data) are created by Docker, owned by root: create them as sal first.
  • docker compose down -v and docker volume prune delete the volumes, with the database. Only when removing an app.
  • Containers also bypass outgoing firewall rules: a container can connect anywhere on the internet. Put databases on an internal network.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text: Why we set things up the way we do. The longer reasoning, and the options we dropped, are in the archived Decisions.

docs.title: Why Docker Compose for everything?
docs.text: One way of working for every app: its whole setup is one file you can read, its versions are pinned, and it runs isolated from the server and the other apps. Backups and retention work the same for every app, because every app keeps its data in the same places (Docker Compose).

docs.title: Why /opt, and not /srv?
docs.text: Both are defensible: by the Linux conventions, /opt is for added software and /srv for data a server serves, and an app's folder holds both. What matters is that it is one place, the same on every server: one folder per app, with everything needed to restore it, and one folder for the backup to cover. Splitting an app over two places would lose that.

docs.title: Why the sal account?
docs.text: So that the apps' files belong to neither a person nor root. Files owned by a personal account break when that person leaves; files owned by root can only be changed with full root rights, and every mistake runs as root. With one system account without a login, every admin works on every app the same way (sudo -u sal, sudoedit -u sal), and the secrets in .env are readable only by sal. You could use root instead; we prefer not to.

docs.title: Why Docker with sudo, and not the docker group?
docs.text: Anyone who can run Docker can mount the whole disk into a container, so the docker group is root access without a password and without logging. sudo asks, and logs.

docs.title: Why only ports on 127.0.0.1?
docs.text: Docker sends traffic to containers around the server's own firewall, so a port published on all addresses is open to the internet, whatever the firewall says. On 127.0.0.1, only the reverse proxy on the same server can reach the app (Pitfalls).

docs.title: Why database dumps, and not a backup of the volumes?
docs.text: A copy of a running database's files can be inconsistent; a dump can't. The app dumps its own database (a service in its compose file), so the backup job doesn't need to know anything about the apps, and never runs app commands as root.

docs.title: Why restic and healthchecks.io?
docs.text: restic encrypts on the server, before anything leaves it, only stores changes, and checks its own backups. healthchecks.io notices a backup that failed and also one that didn't run at all, without the server needing email credentials.

docs.title: Why Keycloak?
docs.text: One login service for all our apps, with separate realms (logins) in one installation, a second factor, and the standard (OIDC) that our own software expects (Authentication standard). It is widely used and maintained, and the lab's admins can reset a member's second factor. We compared others in the archived Provider comparison.

docs.title: Why our own lab portal, and not oauth2-proxy?
docs.text: The lab server needed a start page and a way to handle lab membership anyway, and that app could also do the login, with a few extra features. Who may use which app, and with or without a second factor, is set in a file on the server, which the portal turns into Caddy's configuration. It is a plain OIDC client of Keycloak, like AmCAT and AnnoTinder (deploy-lab-portal).

docs.title: Why is everything under lab. signed in with one login?
docs.text: So that members sign in once, and signing out ends it everywhere. The login cookie is valid for everything under lab.societal-analytics.nl, so only apps the lab runs on its own servers may get an address there, never a site hosted by someone else.

docs.title: Why are our images on GitHub, and public?
docs.text: Our deployments are open source, like the rest of our software. GitHub Actions builds them from the repository and publishes them in the GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io), so a server only downloads an image, and anyone can check what it contains. (Keycloak is the exception: its two images are thin layers on the official ones, built on the server in seconds.)

docs.title: Why is the Keycloak repository private?
docs.text: It holds the login flows and settings of every realm, which nobody outside the lab reviews. A mistake in them would be easy to spot for anyone reading the files, including automated scans. Our other repositories hold general-purpose code; our settings for them stay on the servers.

docs.title: Why is this documentation so short?
docs.text: It describes what we do, for people who know how to run a server. The earlier, step-by-step version is in the archive.

docs.title: Setting up a server
docs.text: The same on every server, physical or VM. A VM on VU SciCloud is created as on University VMs, which also has a script for the first steps.

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
• Ubuntu LTS, with automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades).
  • A personal admin account per person, with sudo and SSH keys. No root logins and no passwords over SSH.
  • Firewall: only ports 80 and 443 open to everyone, SSH only from the VU network.
  • Docker Engine with the compose plugin, from Docker's own repository. Admins run it with sudo; nobody is in the docker group.
How we do it

On a VM, setup-vm.sh does all of the above (University VMs). By hand, the SSH part is:

printf 'PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
' | sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh

Test a new login in a second terminal before closing the first.

docs.title: Apps in /opt
docs.text:
Every app gets a folder /opt/<app> with its compose.yml, its settings (.env) and its data, and runs with Docker Compose (Docker Compose). The folders are owned by a system account, sal, without a login; admins are in its group.

Once per server, create sal and add each admin to its group:

$ sudo useradd --system --home-dir /nonexistent --no-create-home --shell /usr/sbin/nologin sal
$ sudo usermod -aG sal jane
$ id sal
uid=999(sal) gid=999(sal) groups=999(sal)

For each app, e.g. AnnoTinder:

$ sudo mkdir /opt/annotinder
$ sudo chown sal:sal /opt/annotinder && sudo chmod 750 /opt/annotinder
$ cd /opt/annotinder
$ sudo -u sal curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ccs-amsterdam/annotinder/v0.9.0/compose.yml
$ sudo -u sal curl -fsSL -o .env https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ccs-amsterdam/annotinder/v0.9.0/.env.example
$ sudo -u sal chmod 600 .env
$ sudoedit -u sal .env
$ ls -la
total 20
drwxr-x--- 2 sal  sal  4096 Nov 26 10:49 .
drwxr-xr-x 4 root root 4096 Nov 26 10:49 ..
-rw------- 1 sal  sal  4763 Nov 26 10:49 .env
-rw-r--r-- 1 sal  sal  5644 Nov 26 10:49 compose.yml
$ sudo docker compose pull && sudo docker compose up -d
  • 750 on the folder: admins (the sal group) can look inside, other accounts can't. 600 on .env: only sal reads the secrets; admins use sudo.
  • Work as sal: sudo -u sal <command>, and edit with sudoedit -u sal <file> (your own editor, saved as sal). Plain sudo inside /opt/<app> leaves files owned by root.
  • Docker with sudo: sudo docker compose ..., from the app's folder.
  • Folders the app mounts (e.g. data/): create them as sal before the first start (sudo -u sal mkdir data); Docker would create them owned by root.
Why sal, and not root or your own account?

Files owned by a personal account break when that person leaves; files owned by root can only be changed with full root rights. With one system account, every admin works on every app the same way, and nothing in /opt needs root except Docker itself. sal is not in the docker group, since that is effectively root access. More: FAQ.

Updating an app: change the version in compose.yml (or download the compose file of the new version), then sudo docker compose pull && sudo docker compose up -d. Removing one: sudo docker compose down -v (this deletes its volumes, so its database too), then sudo rm -r /opt/<app>.

docs.title: A reverse proxy
docs.text:
Only the reverse proxy (Caddy, with certificates from Let's Encrypt) is reachable from outside; apps listen on 127.0.0.1 or on internal Docker networks. Where it comes from depends on the server:

  • A server with one app (Keycloak, AmCAT, AnnoTinder): the Caddy that comes with the app's compose file.
  • The lab server, with many apps: the lab portal, which is Caddy plus a small app that adds the lab's login to apps that have none.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Every server runs the same nightly backup: deploy-backup, in /opt/backup. It backs up all of /opt with restic, encrypted, after checking that every app's database dumps (/opt/<app>/backups) are recent, and reports to healthchecks.io, which emails us when a backup failed or didn't run.

sudo git clone https://github.com/vu-societal-analytics/deploy-backup.git /opt/backup
sudo /opt/backup/setup.sh https://hc-ping.com/<the server's check>

Then store the encryption password (sudo cat /etc/restic/password) in the lab's password manager. Checks, restores and settings: the deploy-backup README.

So everything needed to restore an app is in /opt/<app>: its compose file and .env, its files in data/, and its database dumps in backups/. Databases are dumped by the app itself (Docker Compose). Every night the new backups are also copied off-site, encrypted, to a Cloudflare R2 bucket per server, which can't be deleted from the server for 30 days (Off-site copy). The server backups of VU IT are the last resort.

docs.title: University VMs (SciCloud)
docs.text:
How to set up a virtual machine (VM) on VU SciCloud, the VU's research cloud, and secure it before hosting anything on it. We use them for the Keycloak, AmCAT and AnnoTinder servers (Our servers). SciCloud is documented by VU Research Data Management (SciCloud, logging in).

Steps 3 to 5 in one script

After creating the VM and logging in as root (steps 1 and 2), setup-vm.sh does steps 3 to 5: your admin user with your SSH keys, the firewall rules, automatic security updates and Docker, and the system account sal for the apps. It can safely run again. Download it, read it, and run it:

cd /tmp && curl -fsSLO https://vu-societal-analytics.github.io/societal-analytics-lab-infra/install/setup-vm.sh

less setup-vm.sh

bash setup-vm.sh <username> --web --ssh-from <VU range 1>,<VU range 2>

--web opens ports 80 and 443 (for a VM that hosts a website or service); --ssh-from <range>,<range> allows SSH only from those ranges, e.g. the VU network (SSH only from the VU network), after checking that your own connection comes from one of them. At the end, it asks you to check in a second terminal that you can log in as your new user and use sudo. Only then, turn off root and password logins:

sudo bash /tmp/setup-vm.sh --harden-ssh

The steps below describe what it does, and are the way to do it by hand.

docs.title: 1. Create the VM
docs.text:
Log in to the VM portal at one.labs.vu.nl, from the VU network or the VU VPN.

Public SSH keys. Go to your profile settings (bottom left), then Security, and add your public SSH key(s). They are added to new VMs when they are created.

Create the VM:

  1. Go to Instances → VMs in the left sidebar, and click Create VM (top right).
  2. Choose a template: the latest Ubuntu LTS version (currently Ubuntu 26.04), in one of two variants:
    • (intern): the VM only gets an address inside the VU network. From outside, nothing on it can be reached, whatever its firewall says.
    • (extern): the VM gets a public internet address, e.g. to host a website or service. What can be reached then depends entirely on the VM's own firewall, and the template allows SSH from anywhere: restrict it in step 4.
  3. Settings:
    • A name for the VM.
    • Turn on Instantiate as persistent for a long-running server that stores data (see Persistence).
    • Memory and CPU: what the services on the VM need. For instance, Keycloak needs about 2 GB of memory.
  4. Click Next, and Finish (bottom right).

docs.title: 2. Log in
docs.text:
The VM is listed under Instances; open it to see its IP address. The default user of the Ubuntu templates is root.

From the VU network or the VU VPN:

ssh root@<ip address>

From elsewhere, via the VU SSH gateway (you first log in with your VUnetID and password):

ssh -J <VUnetID>@ssh.data.vu.nl root@<ip address>

If you ever lose access over SSH, the VM's console in the portal still works with a password.

docs.title: 3. Secure SSH logins
docs.text:
Create your own user with administrator rights (sudo), log in with SSH keys only, and turn off logins as root over SSH.

Create a user. Replace username with your own username:

adduser username

usermod -aG sudo username

Give the user your SSH key. The portal added your key(s) for root, so copy those:

mkdir -p /home/username/.ssh && cp /root/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/username/.ssh/

chown -R username:username /home/username/.ssh && chmod 700 /home/username/.ssh && chmod 600 /home/username/.ssh/authorized_keys

Test before you continue. Keep your current session open, and log in as the new user in a second terminal. Check that sudo works:

ssh username@<ip address>

sudo -v

Only continue when this works, otherwise you can lock yourself out.

Turn off root and password logins over SSH. Put the settings in their own file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/. Settings in that folder take precedence over the main configuration file, and on Ubuntu a file in that folder may already turn password logins on, which would silently undo a change to the main file. Files are read in alphabetical order and the first value wins, so the name starts with 00-:

printf 'PermitRootLogin no\nPasswordAuthentication no\nKbdInteractiveAuthentication no\n' | sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf

Check the configuration, and restart SSH (on Ubuntu the service is called ssh):

sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl restart ssh

Check the settings that are actually in effect. This should show no for all three:

sudo sshd -T | grep -E '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|kbdinteractiveauthentication) '

Then check, in a new terminal, that logging in as root over SSH is refused, and logging in as your own user still works.

docs.title: 4. Firewall
docs.text:
The VMs filter network traffic with iptables, using VU's own setup: the rules are in /etc/iptables-custom, and are loaded with the iptables-custom command. By default, outgoing and incoming traffic may be restricted.

Open the file:

sudo nano /etc/iptables-custom

The file contains VU-specific rules (e.g. access to university services). Leave those in place, and only add the rules you need. Check first whether a rule is already there, to avoid duplicates.

Outgoing web traffic (needed for package updates, git clone and APIs). Under # Filter traffic sent by me:

# Allow outbound web traffic (HTTP/HTTPS) for package managers and APIs
-A OUTBOUND -m state --state NEW -p tcp -m multiport --dports 80,443 -j ACCEPT

Incoming web traffic (if the VM hosts a website or service). Under # Services to the world; with an (extern) template these rules are probably already there:

# Allow inbound web traffic
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 80 -j ACCEPT
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT

docs.title: SSH only from the VU network
docs.text:
On an (extern) VM, SSH is reachable from the whole internet: anyone can try to log in, or try a flaw in SSH itself. Keys-only logins (step 3) make guessing useless, but SSH still runs code for every connection, before any login. So allow SSH only from the VU network (campus and VPN, which includes the VU SSH gateway), and keep ports 80 and 443 open to everyone. (More options for later: Hardening plan.)

Your VU ranges: the address ranges of the VU network and VPN, as found for the admin restriction of Keycloak (Find your IP ranges). Like the rest of the firewall file, they stay on the VM, not in this documentation.

Replace the general SSH rule. Find it under # Services to the world: a rule with --dport 22 and without -s, e.g. -A INBOUND -p tcp --dport 22 -j ACCEPT. Remove it, and add one rule per VU range in its place:

# SSH only from the VU network (campus and VPN, including the VU SSH gateway)
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 22 -s <VU range 1> -j ACCEPT
-A INBOUND -m state --state NEW -m tcp -p tcp --dport 22 -s <VU range 2> -j ACCEPT

Apply it with a safety net: keep your current SSH session open (connected via the VU network or VPN), apply the rules (below), and check that a new login via the VU VPN still works before closing the old one. If something goes wrong, the VM's console in the portal is the way back.

Check from outside: on a phone on mobile data (Wi-Fi off, no VU VPN), ssh <user>@<ip address> (or nc -vz -w 5 <ip address> 22 on a laptop outside the VU) should now time out, while the website still loads.

docs.title: Apply and check
docs.text:
The VMs don't use the standard Ubuntu firewall packages; load the rules with:

sudo iptables-custom

Check the rules that are in effect, for outgoing and incoming traffic:

sudo iptables -S OUTBOUND

sudo iptables -S INBOUND

These rules apply to programs running on the VM itself (e.g. apt, git, curl). They don't apply to Docker containers: see the next section.

docs.title: Docker and the VM firewall
docs.text:
The INBOUND and OUTBOUND rules above don't apply to Docker containers: see Docker Compose.

Reloading the firewall while Docker runs. Check that sudo iptables-custom doesn't remove Docker's own rules. With a container running that publishes ports, the following should show rules for those ports, both before and after sudo iptables-custom:

sudo iptables -t nat -S DOCKER

If the rules are gone after sudo iptables-custom, restart Docker to restore them (running containers restart too):

sudo systemctl restart docker

To verify: on our VM, Docker's chains were still present after sudo iptables-custom, but this still needs to be checked with a container running that publishes ports.

docs.title: 5. Updates and Docker
docs.text:
Security updates. Ubuntu installs security updates automatically with unattended-upgrades. Check that it is installed and enabled:

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades

sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

Some updates (e.g. a new kernel) need a reboot. Ubuntu shows *** System restart required *** when you log in; reboot at a convenient moment. Services started with restart: unless-stopped in Docker Compose come back by themselves.

Docker. Install Docker Engine with the compose plugin, following the official instructions for Ubuntu.

sudo docker compose version

Run Docker with sudo, and don't add users to the docker group: it is effectively root access (see Docker Compose).

docs.title: Persistence
docs.text:
To decide whether to use Instantiate as persistent, it helps to know how the portal combines templates, instances and images:

  • Instances are the actual virtual machines.
  • Images are the storage used by a VM: the operating system, swap space, or additional disks.
  • Templates are recipes for VMs. You create an instance by instantiating a template.

Persistence is a property of images, and determines what happens to them when an instance is created and terminated:

Non-persistent image Persistent image When an instance is created The instance gets a disposable copy of the image The instance is linked to the image itself When the instance is terminated The copy is deleted, including all configuration and data The image remains, so the instance can be created again Parallel instances Possible Not possible Use for Temporary machines, e.g. for testing Servers whose configuration or data must not be lost

What "Instantiate as persistent" does: it first makes a copy of the template with persistent copies of its images, and then creates an instance from that copy. If the instance is ever terminated, you can recover it: go to Templates → VMs, find the template with the same name as the instance, and use Instantiate (not Instantiate as persistent).

Persistence is not a backup

A persistent image survives a terminated VM, but not a broken disk, a deleted image, or a mistake on the VM itself. Servers with data still need backups (Backups).
